passages.title: The earth convulses and testifies
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah az-Zalzalah 99:1–5 — The earth convulses and testifies

These five ayat set a single scene: the ground beneath our feet — the one thing we take to be permanently still — is shaken, empties out what it has been holding, and then, at Allah's command, speaks. What binds them together is a movement from **violence** to **speech**: the earth first heaves (ayah 1), then throws out its burdens (ayah 2), leaving man baffled and questioning (ayah 3); and the answer to his question comes not as an explanation but as testimony — the earth itself declaring its information (ayah 4), because its Lord has inspired it to do so (ayah 5).

## The sūrah a man asked for when he wanted something comprehensive

Before the scene itself, it is worth knowing how weighty this sūrah was held to be.

Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad narrated from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr that a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "Teach me what to recite, O Messenger of Allah!" The Prophet ﷺ told him to recite three of the sūrahs beginning with *Alif, Lām, Rā*. The man replied, "I have become old in age, my heart has hardened and my tongue has become harsh." He was told to recite from those beginning with *Ḥā-Mīm*; he said the same. He was told to recite three of the *Musabbiḥāt*; he said the same again. Then the man asked for "something to recite that is comprehensive" of all of these. So the Prophet ﷺ told him to recite *Idhā zulzilat al-arḍu zilzālahā*. When the Prophet ﷺ finished reciting the sūrah to him, the man said, "By He Who has sent you with the truth as a Prophet, I will never add anything else to it," and turned away and left. The Prophet ﷺ said, **"The little man has been successful, the little man has been successful."** Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i recorded this ḥadīth.

Sit with that. An old man with a hardened heart and a harsh tongue asks for the one thing he can carry — something comprehensive, that gathers it all up — and he is given *this* sūrah. The five ayat before us are how it opens.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report from Sayyidnā Anas and Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Sūrah al-Zilzāl equals half the Qur'an, Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ a third, and Sūrah al-Kāfirūn a quarter — transmitted, as Maʿārif names it, by al-Tirmidhī, al-Baghawī and al-Mazharī.

## Ayah 1: which shaking is this?

**"When the earth is shaken ˹in˺ its ultimate quaking."**

Ibn Kathir cites Ibn ʿAbbās on this ayah: "This means that it will move from beneath it." The very floor of the world is moved out from under itself.

But which convulsion is meant? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazharī) is honest that the scholars did not settle this: it is not clear whether this earthquake refers to the convulsion that will take place in the world **before the first blowing of the trumpet**, mentioned in connection with the portents of the Day of Judgement, or to the quake that will occur **after the second blowing**, when the dead are resurrected and thrown out of their graves. Narratives and the views of the commentators differ on the issue. Maʿārif adds that it is not inconceivable that many quakes and convulsions occur — one before the first blowing, another after the second at the time of raising the dead. It then leans to the second: here it probably refers to the second quake, and the context supports it, since the sūrah later describes the scenes of the Day of Resurrection — reckoning, the weighing and evaluating of deeds, and recompense. And it closes, as the scholars do with such matters, with *Allāhu aʿlam* — Allah knows best.

That is worth imitating. Where the early authorities left a question open, we hold it open too.

## Ayah 2: the earth empties itself

**"And when the earth throws out ˹all˺ its contents."**

Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "the earth throws out its burdens" and explains: it means it will throw forth **that which is in it of the dead**, and he notes that more than one of the Salaf said this. He places the ayah alongside Allah's words, *"O mankind! Have Taqwa of your Lord! Verily, the earthquake (Zalzalah) of the Hour is a terrible thing"* (22:1), and *"And when the earth is stretched forth, and has cast out all that was in it and became empty"* (84:3–4).

There is a second burden the earth has been carrying, and it is one we spend our lives digging for. Ibn Kathir cites that **Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ** from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "The earth will throw out the pieces of its liver (its contents). Gold and silver will come out like columns. A murderer will come and say, 'I killed for this?' The one who broke the ties of kinship will say, 'For this I severed the ties of kinship?' The thief will say, 'For this I got my hands amputated?' Then they will leave it there and no one will take anything from it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this same ḥadīth from Muslim's Ṣaḥīḥ under this ayah.

Read the scene slowly. The gold is *finally* lying in the open, in columns, unguarded — and nobody takes any of it. Every man who priced his soul against it stands there recalculating out loud: *for this?* This is not a teaching that wealth is evil; it is a warning about **the exchange rate**. A murder, a severed kinship, a hand amputated — and on the day the accounting is honest, the thing purchased is left lying there, and no one takes anything from it. The three examples are pointed: the taking of life, the tearing of family bonds, the taking of property. These are the crimes people commit *for* what the earth has been holding.

## Ayah 3: the question nobody can answer

**"And humanity cries, 'What is wrong with it?'"**

One short line, and it is the human heart of the passage. Ibn Kathir explains: he will be **baffled by its situation after it used to be stable, settled and firm, and he used to be settled upon its surface**.

This is precisely the shock. Our whole sense of security rests, without our ever examining it, on the assumption that the ground does not move. We say "solid ground", "firm footing", "settled". Man's cry here is not a theological objection; it is the sound of the last certainty giving way. Ibn Kathir gathers the whole moment: this refers to the alteration of the state of things and the earth moving and shaking; there will come to it an inescapable quaking that Allah prepared for it; then it will throw out its dead — from the first to the last generations; at that time the people will be baffled by the events, and by the earth changing into other than the earth, and the heavens as well. Then they will be presented before Allah, **the One, the Irresistible**.

Note that the question is left hanging in ayah 3. Man asks *what is the matter with it?* — and the next ayah does not answer him. It turns instead to the earth, and lets *it* speak.

## Ayah 4: the ground gives evidence

**"On that Day the earth will recount everything."**

Ibn Kathir renders it, "That Day it will declare its information," and his gloss is plain: it means **it will speak of what the people did upon its surface**.

Ibn Kathir cites that Imam Ahmad, At-Tirmidhī and Abu ʿAbdur-Raḥmān An-Nasa'i all recorded a ḥadīth from Abu Hurayrah — the wording being An-Nasa'i's — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this ayah and then said, **"Do you know what is its information?"** They said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said:

> "Verily, its information is that it will testify against every male and female servant, about what they did upon its surface. It will say that he did such and such on such and such day. So this is its information."

Ibn Kathir adds that At-Tirmidhī said of this ḥadīth: **"Ṣaḥīḥ Gharīb."**

Take in what is being said. The witness here is **the place itself**, and it testifies with dates: *he did such and such, on such and such a day*. Every floor you have stood on, every room, every street, every patch of ground where something was said or taken or done in private — the surface upon which people act is a witness that can be made to speak of what was done upon it. And the testimony is "against every male and female servant": nobody is left out of it.

## Ayah 5: because your Lord inspired it

**"Having been inspired by your Lord ˹to do so˺."**

Here the passage supplies the cause and hands everything back to Allah. The earth does not testify on its own initiative; it speaks because **your Lord** inspired it.

Ibn Kathir says: it is apparent that the implied meaning here is that **He will permit it**. He then gathers the early authorities:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** — narrated by Shabīb bin Bishr from ʿIkrimah — on ayah 4: "Its Lord will say to it, 'Speak.' So it will speak."
- **Mujāhid**, on "inspire it": "He commands it" — that is, He commands it to speak.
- **Al-Qurazī**: "He will command it to separate from them."

We affirm this as Allah has said it, without likening His speaking to His creation to the speech of creatures and without explaining the ayah away: at His word, the earth speaks. The same Lord who prepared for the earth the inescapable quaking of ayah 1 gives it its speech in ayah 4. And note that the ayah does not say merely "a Lord" — it says **your Lord**.

## Living it

The passage does not need a moral appended to it; it *is* one. But three things follow directly from what the sources say here.

**Nothing you stand on is neutral.** If the ground testifies to what was done upon its surface, and testifies with dates, then privacy as we imagine it does not exist. There is no unwitnessed room. That should frighten a person out of hidden sin and comfort a person whose quiet good deeds nobody ever saw — the same witness speaks of what was done, whatever it was.

**Re-price what you are digging for.** The scene in ayah 2 is a mercy given in advance: you are being shown, now, the moment when the murderer, the one who cut the ties of kinship, and the thief look at the gold and say *for this?* You are allowed to run that calculation today, while the exchange can still be refused.

**Ask the question in ayah 3 before it is forced on you.** "What is the matter with it?" is asked too late — after the ground has already gone. The believer who reads this sūrah asks the question early, and the answer is in ayah 5: **because your Lord inspired it**. Everything on that Day, down to the speech of the earth, runs on His command.

The old man in the ḥadīth heard this sūrah once, said he would never add anything else to it, and turned away — and the Prophet ﷺ called him successful. That is the measure of what we have been reading.

passages.title: People shown their deeds, atom by atom
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat bring the surah home. The earlier ayat have described the earth quaking, throwing out its burdens, and declaring its information (ayat 1–5). Now the attention turns from the shaking earth to the human being who lived on it. Ayah 6 shows people moving off from the Judgement in separated groups, that they may be shown their deeds; ayat 7 and 8 tell us the resolution at which that showing happens — down to the weight of a speck of dust, good and evil alike. What holds the passage together is a single movement: from the vast public gathering to the utterly private ledger of one soul.

## Ayah 6: the crowd becomes categories

**"On that Day people will proceed in separate groups."** Ibn Kathir explains the phrase — "That Day mankind will proceed in scattered groups (*Ashtat*)" — as meaning **"they will return from the station of the Judgement in separate groups."** This is not the gathering; it is what comes after it, the moment the standing is over and everyone moves off toward where they belong.

And the groups are not random. Ibn Kathir continues: "This means that they will be divided into types and categories: between those who are miserable and those who are happy, and those who are commanded to go to Paradise and those who are commanded to go to the Hellfire." **As-Suddi** said, "*Ashtat* means sects" — distinct parties, each with its own identity and destination.

The point to feel here: in this life people are mixed. Believer and disbeliever share a street, a marketplace, sometimes a family table. That mixture is temporary. Ayah 6 is the moment the mixture is undone, and every person walks off in the company his deeds earned him.

## "That they may be shown their deeds"

On the closing phrase of the ayah — *li-yuraw a'mālahum*, "that they may be shown their deeds" — Ibn Kathir's gloss is: **"so that they may act and be rewarded for what they did in this life of good and evil."**

Notice how much that carries. The showing is not a spectacle staged for its own sake. It issues in acting and in being recompensed; the seeing *is* the beginning of the reckoning. And notice the wording of the ayah itself: people are *shown* their deeds. The record is not something a person assembles and submits — it is presented to him. Then ayat 7 and 8 close the circuit from the other side: whoever does an atom's weight of good or evil **"shall see it."** Shown, and seeing. There is no possibility of a person failing to recognise his own file.

## Ayat 7–8: the weight of an atom

**"So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it."**

Ibn Kathir renders the measure as **"the weight of a speck of dust"**; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "the weight of a particle." Think of dust motes turning in a shaft of sunlight — something so small you would never think to count it. That is the unit of account.

The two ayat are built as mirror images. Same verb, same measure, same outcome; only "good" and "evil" are exchanged. That symmetry is itself part of the message: the standard of precision does not soften on either side. Nothing is too small to be weighed, in your favour or against you.

Ibn Kathir heads this section **"The Recompense for Every Minute Deed,"** and gathers around it a striking body of Sunnah.

## The ayah the Prophet ﷺ called single and comprehensive

**Al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah** the long hadith of the horses: "The horses are for three. For one man they are a reward, for another man they are a shield, and for another man they are a burden." For the man who keeps them to be used in the way of Allah, "whatever afflicts them during that lengthy period in the pasture or garden, it will be counted as good deeds for him"; and if they are used for a noble battle or two, "their hoof prints and their dung are counted as good deeds for him"; and when they pass through a stream and drink from it, "though he (their owner) does not intend to quench their thirst, yet, it would be counted as good deeds." The man who keeps them to maintain himself and be independent of others, without forgetting the right of Allah upon them, has a shield from the Fire. The man who keeps them "in order to boast, brag and show off" carries a burden.

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about donkeys, and he said: **"Allah has not revealed anything concerning them except this single, comprehensive Ayah"** — and he recited *"So whosoever does good equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it. And whosoever does evil equal to the weight of a speck of dust shall see it."* **Muslim also recorded this Hadith.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that **Sayyidnā 'Abdullah Ibn Mas'ūd** said this verse is the most robust and comprehensive verse of the Holy Qur'an, and that **Sayyidnā Anas**, in a lengthy narration, reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ referred to it as *al-fādhdhah al-jāmi'ah* — "the unique, most comprehensive verse."

Sit with what that means. Asked about a matter no revelation had specifically addressed, the answer was not a new ruling but a principle already given — one line covering every question of moral consequence that could be raised. Nothing falls outside it, because nothing is beneath it.

## Never belittle a small good

Because the measure is that fine, the tiny act is never wasted. Ibn Kathir lines up the evidence:

- **In Sahih Al-Bukhari**, from 'Adi, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Fear (ward off) the Fire, even if by giving half a date in charity, and even by saying a single word of good."*
- **In the Sahih as well**, 'Adi narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: *"Do not under rate any good act, even if it is offering drinking water from your bucket to one who is seeking a drink, or meeting your brother with a cheerful face."*
- Also **recorded in the Sahih**, the Prophet ﷺ said: *"O party of believing women! None of you should belittle a gift sent by your neighbor, even if it is a Firsan of a sheep"* — Ibn Kathir notes that *Firsan* here means its hoof.
- And in another hadith he ﷺ said: *"Give something to the beggar, even if it is a burnt hoof."*

Look at what qualifies. Half a date. A single good word. Tipping your bucket into a thirsty person's cup. Meeting your brother with an open face. These are not "acts of worship" as people usually keep score — they cost nothing, they are the small change of daily life. This passage says the small change is legal tender.

Ibn Kathir reports that **'A'ishah** gave a single grape in charity and then said: *"To how much dust is it equivalent?"* She was not weighing whether the gift was worth giving; she was counting how much it came to in the currency of ayah 7.

## Never belittle a small sin

Ayah 8 runs the same arithmetic in the other direction, and the Sunnah is just as insistent.

**Imam Ahmad recorded** from 'Awf bin Al-Harith bin At-Tufayl that 'A'ishah told him the Prophet ﷺ used to say: *"O 'A'ishah! Beware of the sins that are belittled, for indeed they will be taken account of by Allah."* **An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah recorded this Hadith.**

**Imam Ahmad recorded** from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Beware of the sins that are belittled. For verily, they are gathered in a man until they destroy him."*

And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a parable for exactly this — that such sins are like a people who settle in barren land. Their leader comes and orders the men to go out one at a time, each to bring back a stick, until they have gathered a large number of sticks. Then they kindle a fire, and it burns everything they throw into it.

That is the psychology of the small sin, told perfectly. No single stick is a fire. No man carrying one stick believes he is building a blaze. The danger lies not in any one act but in the gathering — and the man who thinks only in single sticks never sees the pile.

## Two qualifications from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important precision to each half of the pair.

**On ayah 7 — what "good" means.** The word "good" here refers to what is good in terms of Sharī'ah: "only a good deed done in the wake of faith is recognized by Allah." A good deed done in a state of disbelief is not recognised, and so will not be rewarded in the Hereafter, though it may be rewarded in this world. A non-believer who has done "tons of good deeds" receives his return for them here, but they are rendered vain in the Hereafter for want of faith.

**And a hope drawn from the same verse.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues from this ayah that anyone who has an atom's weight of faith will eventually be taken out of Hell. The reasoning: the verse promises that a person must reap the fruit of his righteousness in the Hereafter — and if he has done no righteous deeds at all, faith itself is a great righteousness. So no matter how sinful a believer may be, he will not be condemned to Hell for good. The very precision that frightens is also the guarantee that not one particle of faith is overlooked.

**On ayah 8 — what "evil" means.** By "evil" here is meant evil for which the wrongdoer **has not repented**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an and the Sunnah bear ample testimony that Allah most certainly accepts the sincere repentance of any sinner. But the sins a person has not repented of in this world will certainly bring their results, "no matter how trivial or petty they might have been in their appearance." That, Maʿārif adds, is precisely why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ warned Sayyidah 'A'ishah to beware of the sins that are belittled.

So the two ayat are not a mechanical scale a person is simply trapped inside. Ayah 7 is opened by faith; ayah 8 is closed by repentance. Between those two doors, the weighing is exact.

## Living it

The practical demand of this passage is a change in what you consider worth counting.

Most of us keep a private mental ledger with a minimum entry size: the prayer counts, the donation counts — but the smile does not, and neither does the small sharpness in the voice. Ayat 7 and 8 abolish the minimum entry size. Everything is recorded at the weight of a speck of dust, and on the Day of ayah 6 the whole file is shown to you, and you see it.

Which turns the fear inside out, if you let it. If nothing is too small to be counted against you, then nothing is too small to be counted for you either. A single grape is worth calculating. Half a date wards off the Fire. A cheerful face when you meet your brother goes into the record. And no single stick is worth carrying home, because you have seen what the pile becomes.
